items.text: Why deals break · The full list
Seventy-five signed letters, and the reason each one died.
A finding outside the earnings work
A license, a contract, a compliance gap, a customer concentration. 19.1 percent in 2023 and 21.5 percent in 2024.
The earnings were not what was presented
Adjusted earnings that did not survive the source documents. 10.6 percent in 2023: the share doubled in two years.
The renegotiation that followed
The finding did not kill the deal. The argument about the price after it did.
The seller walked
The owner withdrew under exclusivity, for reasons the study records as the seller’s own.
Financing
The buyer could not fund the deal. 21.3 percent in 2023, so the share halved as rates settled.
Underperformance
The business fell short of its own numbers between the letter and the closing date.

sections.name: Half of what ends a signed deal was in the records before the letter.

items.text: Why deals break · What it means
Half of what ends a signed deal was in the records before the letter.
What the two studies are

The first is a lower-middle-market deal platform’s report on seventy-five of its own transactions that reached a signed letter of intent in 2025 and did not close, across eight buyer types and eight industries, with the reason each buyer or adviser reported. The percentages are separate categories of a single list, so they can be read together: nearly half of the broken letters ended on something diligence found, in the earnings or outside them, and a further seventh ended on the renegotiation that followed a finding.

The second is a study of what happens after closing: the claims buyers make against the escrow when a representation turns out to have been wrong. A claim for an undisclosed liability is a finding that diligence missed. Its share of all claims doubled in two years, it takes longer to resolve than any other kind, and it is three times as likely to end in front of a judge or an arbitrator.
Half of what ends a signed deal was in the records before the letter was signed. The other finding, the one that surfaces after closing, was in the same records.
Our read
The valuation gap, before any of this

Deals that never reach a letter die on price. In the 2024 Pepperdine survey of investment bankers, a valuation gap was the reason 49 percent of their engagements did not close, and two thirds of those gaps were between 11 and 30 percent of the price. In the 2026 lower-middle-market outlook, valuation expectations were the leading cause of failed deals at 28.3 percent, with diligence findings second at 24.5 percent. An owner’s number and a buyer’s number are built from the same records; the gap between them is what the records support and what they do not.
What the findings have in common

A license that does not transfer. A contract with a change-of-control clause nobody read. A customer that is 30 percent of revenue. An add-back with no document behind it. Revenue recognized when the cash arrived rather than when it was earned. None of these is hidden. Each is in a document the company already holds, and each is found in the sixth week of exclusivity by a buyer’s team that is paid to find it. The difference between a deal that closes and one that does not is often only who read the document first.

For a buyer, that is the case for having the evidence on a target assembled before the letter is priced, so that the price already reflects the findings. For an owner, it is the case for reading the records the way a buyer will, while there is still time to fix what they show. The public record of signed deals that died, with the court opinions and filings behind each one, is in the Dead Deal Notes.
